01.note: Rabbi Eliezer recalls a girl in the village of Hitlo who stopped menstruating for three cycles and then bled again. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that 'her time is sufficient': she is impure only from the moment she saw blood, not retroactively. The other Sages answered Rabbi Eliezer that a ruling made in exigent circumstances is no proof. The Gemara gives two accounts of the emergency: some say it was during years of famine, others that the girl had handled many ritually pure items and the Sages did not want them all lost.
01.why: The mishna records Rabbi Eliezer's view that any woman who goes three cycles without bleeding is impure only from the time she sees blood; this incident is his proof. The Gemara next tells how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi relied on Rabbi Eliezer in exactly such an emergency.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who cites the incident as proof for his ruling, against the other Sages.

terms.meaning: A woman whose status this describes becomes impure only from the moment she sees blood. Otherwise, a woman can be treated as impure retroactively, so that pure items she touched in the preceding hours become impure.
An emergency or time of great need, when the Sages might rule leniently. The other Sages argue that such a ruling cannot serve as a precedent for ordinary times.
Food and objects kept in a state of ritual purity, which become unusable for that purpose if touched by someone impure.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

02.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once ruled in a case according to the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer. After he remembered, he said: Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon in exigent circumstances. The Gemara then asks what 'after he remembered' means: if he remembered that the law had been decided against Rabbi Eliezer, how could he follow him even in an emergency?
02.why: The Sages had just dismissed Rabbi Eliezer's precedent as an emergency ruling. The Gemara answers its question by explaining that no ruling had yet been fixed; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi remembered that many Sages, not one, disagreed with Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; he ruled as Rabbi Eliezer did and then defended relying on him in an emergency.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose lenient view about a woman who missed three cycles Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi followed.

terms.meaning: An emergency or time of great need, when a lenient minority opinion might be relied upon.
Jewish law, or the binding ruling on a particular question.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

03.note: Rav Yehuda and his teacher Shmuel were standing on the roof of the synagogue in Neharde'a. Rav Yehuda said to Shmuel that he needed to urinate. Shmuel told him: Shinnana, hold your penis and urinate outward, so that the water would fall away from the synagogue roof rather than onto it.
03.why: The Gemara has been warning that a man should not hold his penis, lest he emit semen for naught. It asks how Rav Yehuda could do so, and Abaye answers that fear kept him from sexual thoughts, as frightened marauders are presumed not to pour wine for idols.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Shmuel's student, who needed to urinate while on the synagogue roof.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Yehuda's teacher, who told him how to urinate without wetting the synagogue roof.

terms.meaning: A nickname Shmuel used for Rav Yehuda, usually understood as 'sharp one'.

04.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi kept praising Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa to Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, as a great man, and Rabbi Yishmael asked to meet him. When Rabbi Ḥama came, Rabbi Yishmael invited him to ask a question. Rabbi Ḥama asked about a woman who examined herself with a cloth she had not checked beforehand, put it in a box, and found blood on it the next day. Rabbi Yishmael offered to answer by his father Rabbi Yosei's view or by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's; Rabbi Ḥama chose Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's. Rabbi Yishmael scoffed: is this the great man? How can he set aside the teacher's words and listen to the student's?
04.why: The Gemara has just discussed this very case of blood found on an unchecked cloth in a box. After the story it explains Rabbi Ḥama's choice and identifies the two views: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi deems the woman impure and Rabbi Yosei deems her pure.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called 'Rabbi'; he praised Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa. He had been a student of Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa
people.about: The scholar praised as a great man, who asked the question and chose Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Asked to meet Rabbi Ḥama, then mocked his choice of the student's view over his father's.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Rabbi Yishmael's father, called the teacher of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

terms.meaning: A cloth a woman uses to check herself for menstrual blood. Here it had not been checked for stains before use, so it is unclear where the blood came from.
Jewish law, or the binding ruling on a particular question.

05.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting before a bloodletter for treatment. The bloodletter drew blood from Ameimar into a first horn; Ameimar looked at it and told his colleagues that this is the red that the mishna speaks of. The bloodletter drew more blood into another horn, and Ameimar said its color had changed. Rav Ashi said that a Sage like himself, who cannot tell the one from the other, should not examine blood at all.
05.why: The mishna lists the shades of blood that make a woman impure, and Rav Naḥman has said that its red is like the blood of bloodletting. This scene puts that comparison to the eye and shows how fine the distinctions are.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: The Sage whose blood was drawn and who identified the mishna's red in it.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A colleague sitting with Ameimar and Rav Ashi before the bloodletter.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Could not see the difference between the two samples and concluded he should not judge blood.

terms.meaning: A horn used by a bloodletter to draw and collect blood, a common medical treatment at the time.
Examining a woman's blood stain to rule whether its color makes her ritually impure or leaves her pure.
The earliest written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

06.note: Ulla held that the black blood the mishna calls impure is like the very black garments worn in Siva'a. When Ulla came to Pumbedita, he saw an Arab dressed in a black garment and told the Sages there that this is the black of the mishna. People tore the garment off the man bit by bit, each wanting a sample of the shade, and paid him four hundred dinars for it.
06.why: The mishna says blood as black as ink is impure, and the Sages are trying to pin down exactly which black it means; Ulla's comparison is one of several, followed by Rabbi Yoḥanan's comparison to the cloths of bath attendants.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage who visited Pumbedita and pointed to the Arab's garment as the mishna's black.

terms.meaning: The earliest written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments. Here it lists the colors of blood that make a woman impure.

07.note: A woman brought blood to Rabbi Elazar for examination while Rabbi Ami was sitting before him. Rabbi Elazar smelled it and told her it was blood of desire, not menstrual blood. After she left, Rabbi Ami caught up with her and asked about her situation. She told him her husband had been away on a journey and she had desired him. Rabbi Ami applied to Rabbi Elazar the verse 'The counsel of the Lord is with those who fear Him.'
07.why: Ulla had just refused to examine blood in Pumbedita, citing Rabbi Elazar, 'the master of the Land of Israel', who would not examine blood away from home. The Gemara asks why he had that title, and this story is the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Called the master of the Land of Israel; he identified the blood by its smell.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's student, who checked with the woman and confirmed his teacher's ruling.

terms.meaning: Bleeding caused by a woman's longing for her husband rather than by menstruation, and so not making her impure.

08.note: Ifera Hurmiz, mother of King Shapur, was keeping the laws of menstruation and sent blood to Rava to examine. With Rav Ovadya sitting before him, Rava smelled it and told her it was blood of desire. She told her son to see how wise the Jews are; he answered that it may have been a lucky guess. So she sent Rava sixty kinds of blood, and he identified every one except the last, which was lice blood. Without knowing it, he sent her a gift of a comb for killing lice. She exclaimed that the Jews must dwell in the chambers of people's hearts.
08.why: It follows the account of Rabbi Elazar identifying blood of desire by its smell, in a run of stories about the Sages' skill, and caution, in examining blood.

people.name: Ifera Hurmiz
people.about: Mother of King Shapur; she sent blood to Rava and then tested him with sixty samples.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: Ifera Hurmiz's son, who suggested Rava's first answer was a lucky guess.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who examined her blood and identified nearly all the samples.

people.name: Rav Ovadya
people.about: Was sitting before Rava when he examined the blood.

terms.meaning: Bleeding caused by a woman's longing for her husband rather than by menstruation, and so not making her impure.

terms.term: A blind man through a chimney
terms.meaning: A proverb for a lucky hit: a blind man who happens to escape through the one opening.

09.note: Yalta, Rav Naḥman's wife, brought blood to Rabba bar bar Ḥana, who deemed her impure. She then brought it to Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rav Yehuda, who deemed her pure. The Gemara asks how he could, since a baraita teaches that once one authority has declared something impure another may not declare it pure. It explains that at first he too deemed her impure, but she told him that Rabba bar bar Ḥana deems blood of this color pure every day, and ruled otherwise only now because his eye hurt. Then he deemed her pure.
09.why: The Gemara goes on to ask whether a woman is believed when she makes claims like Yalta's about her blood, and later returns to this case as a possible proof.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Naḥman's wife, who took her blood to a second Sage after the first deemed it impure.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: The Sage who deemed her impure; Yalta said his eye was hurting that day.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rav Yehuda
people.about: The second Sage, who deemed her pure after hearing her explanation.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.
Ruled whether the blood's color makes the woman ritually impure as a menstruating woman, which forbids marital relations until she immerses.

10.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi examined a woman's blood at night and deemed it impure. He looked at it again by day and deemed it pure. He waited an hour and deemed it impure again, then said: Woe is me, perhaps I erred! The Gemara objects that he certainly erred, since a baraita teaches that an authority may not reason that the blood would have been impure had it still been moist.
10.why: The Gemara retells the incident so it fits that rule: a judge has only what his eyes see, so each ruling followed what he saw at the time, and the blood was impure but slowly fading. It then turns to how Sages examined blood by light and shade.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called 'Rabbi'; he examined the same blood three times and worried he had ruled wrongly.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

11.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, tells of two cases his father brought from Tivin to the Sages in Yavne. A woman kept discharging things like red shells; people asked his father, his father asked the Sages, and the Sages asked the doctors, who said she had a wound in her womb. The ruling was that she should put them in water, and if they dissolved she is impure. In a second case a woman discharged things like red hairs; the doctors said she had a mole in her womb, and the same water test was given.
11.why: The mishna says a woman who discharges red items like shells or hairs should put them in water to see if they are blood. When the Gemara asks whether such cases ever really happen, these two incidents show that they do.

terms.meaning: Here, the ritual impurity of a menstruating woman: if the items dissolve, they are blood, and she has that status.

12.note: The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya went out to the villages, and when they came back their father asked whether any case had come to them for a ruling. They told him that a woman had miscarried a fetus with a flat face and they had deemed her impure as a woman after childbirth. Rabbi Ḥiyya told them to go out and declare pure what they had declared impure. If they thought they were being strict, he said, it was a stringency that leads to a leniency, because they had also given her the days of purity that follow childbirth.
12.why: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish disagree about a woman who miscarries a fetus whose face is flat; Rabbi Ḥiyya's ruling to his sons treats such a fetus as not a birth at all.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Father of the sons; he reversed their ruling.

people.name: Sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Ruled on the case while away in the villages and were told to undo their ruling.

terms.term: Impurity of a woman after childbirth
terms.meaning: After giving birth a woman is impure for a set period, seven days for a boy and fourteen for a girl, by the Torah's rules.
The weeks after that period of impurity during which, by the Torah's rules, bleeding does not make a woman who has given birth impure.

terms.term: A stringency that leads to a leniency
terms.meaning: A strict ruling that ends up producing a lenient result, here by treating bleeding in the coming weeks as pure.

13.note: A woman discharged something shaped like a snake, and Ḥanina, Rabbi Yehoshua's nephew, ruled her impure as a woman after childbirth. Rabbi Yosef told Rabban Gamliel, who sent word to Rabbi Yehoshua to bring his nephew to him. On the way, Ḥanina's daughter-in-law came out and asked Rabbi Yehoshua about such a case. He said the mother is pure. She replied that her mother-in-law had told her in his name that the mother is impure, because a snake's eye is round like a human's. Her words reminded him, and he sent to Rabban Gamliel: Ḥanina ruled on my authority.
13.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a fetus shaped like a lilith counts as a birth. From this story Abaye learns that a scholar should state the reason for his ruling, so that when reminded of it he will remember the ruling.

people.name: Ḥanina
people.about: Rabbi Yehoshua's nephew, who ruled the woman impure.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Ḥanina's uncle; he had forgotten his own ruling until reminded.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Summoned Rabbi Yehoshua and his nephew over the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yosef
people.about: Reported Ḥanina's ruling to Rabban Gamliel.

terms.term: Impure as a woman after childbirth
terms.meaning: Treating the discharge as a real birth, so the mother has the Torah's period of impurity that follows childbirth.

14.note: Abba Shaul, or some say Rabbi Yoḥanan, recalls his days as a gravedigger. Once he chased a deer and ran into the thighbone of a corpse. He ran after the deer for three parasangs inside it, never caught the deer, and never reached the end of the bone. When he came back, he was told it was the thighbone of Og, king of Bashan.
14.why: Abaye has spoken of undiluted wine harming an embryo, and the Gemara cited Abba Shaul's gravedigger observations on wine and bones; this is another of his gravedigging reports, followed by a third.

people.name: Abba Shaul
people.about: A gravedigger who tells this story about himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Some say the story is his rather than Abba Shaul's.

people.name: Og, king of Bashan
people.about: A giant king from the Bible; the bone was said to be his.

terms.meaning: A Persian measure of distance, roughly a few miles.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

15.note: Abba Shaul recalls his days as a gravedigger. Once a burial cave opened beneath him, and he found himself standing in the eye socket of a corpse, sunk up to his nose. When he came back, he was told it was the eye of Absalom.
15.why: It is the third of Abba Shaul's gravedigger reports. The Gemara then insists he was no midget but the tallest man of his generation, and lists each generation's tallest man, each reaching only the shoulder of the one before.

people.name: Abba Shaul
people.about: A gravedigger who tells this story about himself.

people.name: Absalom
people.about: King David's son in the Bible; the eye was said to be his.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

16.note: A gestational sac a woman had discharged was brought before Mar Shmuel. He said the embryo was forty-one days old. He then counted from the day she had gone to immerse in the ritual bath and found only forty days. He told the court that her husband had had intercourse with her while she was a menstruating woman. They bound the husband, and he confessed.
16.why: Shmuel had ruled that a woman who discharges such a sac must be concerned it was a birth, as if he were unsure. The Gemara asks how he could be unsure given this story, and answers that Shmuel was exceptional; his cautious rule is for others less skilled.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: Shmuel; he dated the embryo exactly and so exposed the husband.

terms.meaning: The membrane that surrounds an early embryo, here discharged in a miscarriage.
A woman immerses in a ritual bath at the end of her menstrual impurity, after which she and her husband may resume relations.
A woman in her period of menstrual impurity, with whom intercourse is forbidden until she immerses.

17.note: Shmuel, Rav's students and Rav Yehuda were sitting together when Rav Yosef, son of Rav Menashya of D'vil, came hurrying toward them. Shmuel remarked that here came a man one could knock down with a straw of wheat, and he would fall and stay down. When Rav Yosef arrived, Shmuel asked him what Rav had said about an afterbirth. He answered that Rav said an afterbirth is attributed only to a viable offspring. Shmuel asked all of Rav's students, and they confirmed it. Then Shmuel looked harshly at Rav Yehuda, a student of Rav who had not passed this teaching on to him.
17.why: The discussion has been about whether an afterbirth discharged after a birth is linked to that birth, and about conflicting reports of what Rav said; this story records Rav's ruling as his students confirmed it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Asked what Rav had said and was annoyed that Rav Yehuda had not told him.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
people.about: The man Shmuel belittled, who then reported Rav's ruling correctly.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A student of Rav who had not passed this ruling on to Shmuel.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose ruling on the afterbirth is in question.

terms.meaning: The placenta and membranes expelled after a birth. The question is whether a separate afterbirth means a second, unseen offspring was miscarried.
A baby that can survive, as opposed to a non-viable newborn.

18.note: The Rabbis told Rabbi Yishmael of Cleopatra, Queen of Alexandria. Her maidservants had been sentenced to death by the government, and she experimented on them to see how long an embryo takes to form; she found that both male and female embryos were formed by the forty-first day. Rabbi Yishmael answered: I bring you proof from the Torah, and you bring me proof from the fools?
18.why: Rabbi Yishmael holds that a male embryo forms in forty-one days and a female in eighty-one, deriving it from the Torah's periods of impurity after birth. The Rabbis cite Cleopatra against him; the Gemara then explains why he called her proof one from fools.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Held that a female embryo takes twice as long to form as a male, and rejected the Rabbis' proof.

people.name: Cleopatra
people.about: Queen of Alexandria, who experimented on her condemned maidservants.

terms.meaning: The point at which an embryo has taken recognizable shape, which affects whether a woman who miscarries counts as having given birth.

19.note: In this telling, Rabbi Yishmael is the one who cites Cleopatra, the Greek queen. Her maidservants had been sentenced to death by the government; she experimented on them and found that a male embryo was formed on the forty-first day and a female on the eighty-first. The Rabbis answered him: One does not bring proof from the fools.
19.why: The Gemara has just discussed a version in which the Rabbis cited Cleopatra against Rabbi Yishmael; this second baraita reverses the roles, and the Gemara goes on to explain why the Rabbis dismissed the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Cites Cleopatra's findings as support for his view.

people.name: Cleopatra
people.about: Called the Greek queen; she experimented on her condemned maidservants.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

20.note: Two people set out on a business trip. A thorn pierced one of them, so he could not go, and he began blaspheming and cursing. Some time later he heard that his companion's ship had sunk at sea, and he began thanking and praising God. That, the teaching concludes, is why the verse says 'Your anger is turned away, and You comfort me.'
20.why: Rav Yosef asks what Isaiah means by 'I will give thanks to You, Lord, for You were angry with me'; this case is his answer. Rabbi Elazar's teaching follows, that even the one a miracle is done for does not recognize it.
